This side of the island has little left. The elders want to cross the mountains to the far side.
The herds have changed their routes. The elders want the band to follow them into land none of you has seen.
Year after year there is not enough food. The children grow thin. The band must decide what to do.
Food shortage and climate change were major forces that spread humans across the world.
A hunter falls from a cliff. His arm is broken and he cannot walk. He will not feed himself for a long time.
The Shanidar 1 fossil from the Zagros had several injuries and disabilities yet lived on for years, which means others cared for him.
Share food and care for him
Cared for an injured friend until he recovered
He survives, and spends years teaching children to make tools.
The band moves on more slowly. You are not sure you did right.
You are one of the oldest in the band. The children want to hear what you know.
Anthropologists find that elders help grandchildren survive, with both food and knowledge.
Teach them to make stone tools
Passed toolmaking on to the grandchildren
Small hands strike stone after you until their fingers bleed, but they remember.
Tell of the lands and herds you have seen
Told the grandchildren the old stories
Your stories will be told after you are gone.
A herd of Columbian mammoths comes down to drink. The biggest stands over four metres tall.
A herd of woolly mammoths crosses the grassland near camp. Every hunter looks at the others.
Sites in eastern Europe and Siberia hold thousands of mammoth bones, some with weapon tips lodged in them, but scientists still debate how often people hunted mammoths and how often they scavenged.
Cut one from the herd and close in with spears
Wait for the vultures, then look for a mammoth dead in the bog
You find a fresh carcass. The band butchers it and carries off the tusks.
The carcass you find has gone bad, and wolves are guarding it.
Let them go and hunt deer instead
Deer are smaller, but nobody has to risk their life.
The steppe has too few trees to build with, but mammoth bones lie everywhere. The elders want a house of bone and tusk, covered in hides.
At Mezhyrich, Ukraine, mammoth-bone dwellings about 15,000 years old used hundreds of bones; an older ring of mammoth bones is known at Kostenki, Russia.
Mammoth jaws stacked into walls, a curved tusk for a doorway. Inside it is warmer than anywhere anyone has slept.
Hide tents are easier to move after the herds.
The cave wall in the dark
You carry a fat lamp deep into the cave. The flicker makes the rock look as if animals hide in it.
At the cave mouth is a smooth rock wall. In your hands are charcoal and red ochre.
The paintings of Chauvet Cave, France, are about 36,000 years old, Lascaux about 17,000, and stencilled hands are found in caves worldwide.
Paint horses and mammoths running across the wall
Painted animals on a cave wall
When the flame trembles, the animals seem to run. The children cannot look away.
Blow red ochre around your own hand on the stone
Left a handprint on a cave wall
Your handprint will outlast every name in the band.
Do not paint; leave the dark quickly
The cave is so quiet you can hear your own heart. You hurry back to the light.
You find a small wolf pup whimpering near camp. Its mother is not coming back.
Dogs were domesticated during the Ice Age; exactly when is debated. A grave at Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, about 14,000 years old, holds a dog buried beside people.
Keep it and feed it scraps
Raised a wolf until it was tame
It grows up and follows you everywhere. On the hunt it smells the game before anyone.
That night you hear it crying for a long time.
The hunter who followed the herds farthest comes back saying that past the ice, along the coast, lies land where no one’s fire burns.
You stay where you know, but the land to the east is talked about every night.
The village will paddle beyond the reef after tuna. Someone asks if you are coming.
A big wave rolls the canoe. You cling to the hull until the others right it. You will never forget that sea.
You help haul the first tuna aboard. Everyone laughs when it slaps you with its tail.
You come back with a pandanus basket full of fish.
Each morning the elders watch birds fly east. A new double-hulled canoe is ready, loaded with pigs, dogs, chickens and plant cuttings.
Earlier generations sailed east many times and never found land. Someone asks if you will try again.
Steer by stars, swells and birds, and search for new land
Wait for a year of westerly winds, then sail
You watch the wind every morning. A year when it turns will make the run east easier.
Stay and tend the taro gardens
Others sail. You watch the sail vanish over the horizon.
The great feast of the island
The chiefs of every village gather. Everyone knows whoever can host this feast will be heeded by the whole island.
In Polynesian societies high chiefs were called ariki (aliʻi in Hawaiʻi and Samoa); their power came from genealogy, ability and giving food away.
Host a feast that feeds every village
Became ariki of the whole island
Dozens of pigs come out of the earth ovens and everyone eats their fill. Your name joins the genealogies recited ever after.
Send a fleet to find new islands for those to come
Sent out a voyaging fleet as ariki
Many canoes leave the bay together, with people from every village aboard.
Go home to your own village
You want nothing more than your own village.
A wayfinder believes that sailing still farther east will reach a land without end.
Sweet potato from South America reached Polynesia before Europeans did, and DNA shows Polynesians and Native South Americans met around 1200 CE.
Reached the South American coast and came home with sweet potato
Weeks later you see a coast that never ends. People on shore trade orange roots for things from the canoe. You bring them home to plant.
A storm drives the canoe off course and the water runs out before any land. It barely makes it home.
All your life you wonder what lies to the east.
The ones who went scouting return with news of the land ahead. Everyone looks to you.
People never set out to cross the world. Each generation moved a few dozen kilometres, following food and climate, until over tens of thousands of years they reached every continent.
The old woman in the mist
One misty dawn an old woman from a band nobody knows holds out a smooth black stone. She says it will give back one life.
The stone is warm, as if alive. When you look up, she is gone.
She laughs softly and walks back into the mist.
Night after night you hear a voice calling from the river. The elders say its spirit wants a gift.
The voice falls silent. In the years after, luck seems oddly on your side.
You laugh at the river. The band admires your nerve, but some nights you still hear it.
Thirty days at sea: no birds, no still clouds, no land. The canoe turns home with half its water left.
On the twenty-third morning seabirds pass the bow, then a cloud that will not move sits on the horizon. That afternoon you step onto a beach no human has ever touched.
A storm tears the sail. Everyone bails all night. The canoe barely makes it home.
The wind is against you. The canoe turns back before the water runs out.
There is no clear evidence of what this species did for its dead; this is a simulation.
Neanderthals buried their dead at several sites, such as La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France and Shanidar Cave in Iraq, though details like flowers in graves are still debated.
At Teouma in Vanuatu, Lapita people buried their dead and later returned to remove or rebury the skulls. Polynesian tradition tells that the spirit journeys back to the ancestors’ homeland.
At Lake Mungo, Australia, about 40,000 years ago, one body was covered in red ochre and another was cremated, the oldest cremation known.
At Sungir, Russia, about 34,000 years ago, bodies were buried sewn with thousands of mammoth-ivory beads.
The child grave at Panga ya Saidi, Kenya, which researchers call “Mtoto”, is about 78,000 years old, the oldest known burial in Africa.
The graves at Qafzeh and Skhul, Israel, about 100,000 years old, are among the oldest burials known; a child at Qafzeh was buried with deer antlers.
Bury them near the house, and one day bring the skull home to the family
Years later the skull rests in the house, close to the descendants.
Hold a rite sending the spirit across the sea to the ancestors’ homeland
Everyone stands on the beach at sunset, looking the way the spirit will travel home.
Everyone sits with the body until morning
No one speaks, but no one leaves either.
Lay the body deep in a cave, away from animals
The cave is utterly silent. They will rest there.
Dig a shallow pit in the cave floor and lay the body curled up
Everyone covers the body gently, as if afraid to hurt them.
Bury them under a scattering of red ochre
The red on the body is like warm blood. The elders say it will carry them to the ancestors.
Bury them with their tools, antlers and beads
Each thing is laid by their hand, in case they need it where they are going.
Burn the body, then bury what bones remain
The smoke rises straight on a windless night. Everyone watches until it is gone.
Sing all night, then let the band move on
The song will be sung again every year on the same night.
The band buries you beneath a tree near camp. Your mother sings you one last lullaby.
No one knows what your people did for their dead. Perhaps they sat with you until morning.
You are buried near the house. Years later your descendants bring your skull home to keep close, believing your spirit has crossed the sea to the ancestors.
The band lays you in a shallow pit in the cave floor, curled as if asleep.
Your body is dusted with red ochre by the lake, as people did at Lake Mungo.
Your clothes are sewn with thousands of mammoth-ivory beads, like the graves at Sungir.
The band digs a grave and scatters red ochre over you.
People paddle in from many islands for the rite.
People from many bands come to the rite, some walking for days.
The whole band sings for you all night.
Things you made with your own hands are laid beside you.
On a rock wall not far away, your hand and your child’s small hand are still side by side.
On a rock wall not far away, your handprint is still there.
Your dog lies by the grave for days.
Your tame wolf lies by the grave for days.
Your children will come back here many times.
The twelfth spear brings it down. The band’s shout rolls across the plain. Meat, fat, hide and bone enough for the whole winter.
Once again a mammoth falls to your band.
The mammoth turns. Its trunk throws you through the air. You live, with several broken ribs.
The mammoth escapes with three spears in its hide. Everyone comes back empty-handed and exhausted.
On a hillside you meet people who are stockier, with heavy brows and big noses, speaking sounds you do not understand.
A group walks up from the south: tall, slim, high foreheads, jutting chins. They stare at you for a long time.
A stocky group comes down from the west. Their tools look like yours, but not quite.
A group comes down from the eastern valleys. They look like you, but their molars are much larger.

Natufians hunted gazelle as a staple for thousands of years, but no one ever domesticated it: it panics, leaps high, and will not live as a herd under people. Most wild animals cannot be domesticated for reasons like these.
Most deer are territorial and skittish, and the males turn violent in the rut. Of all the deer, only reindeer were ever herded, and much later.
At Uan Afuda cave in Libya, about 9,000 years ago, people seem to have penned wild Barbary sheep inside the cave, leaving thick layers of dung, yet Barbary sheep never became truly domestic.

Domestic chickens descend from Southeast Asian junglefowl. Evidence from Ban Non Wat in Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand, shows domestic chickens by about 3,500 years ago, thousands of years after your time, and they may first have been kept for social reasons rather than food.
In New Guinea, cassowary eggshells about 18,000–6,000 years old suggest people collected eggs near hatching to raise the chicks. Grown cassowaries are very dangerous and were never herded.
Wild boar can be tamed, but domestic pigs reached mainland Southeast Asia with farmers from the north thousands of years later.

Turning a wild animal into a domestic one took centuries to millennia, as the tamest were bred generation after generation; the game squeezes this into one life. Goats from Ganj Dareh, Iran, about 10,000 years ago, are among the clearest early domestic goats.

Domestic sheep descend from wild mouflon of Anatolia and the Zagros; it took many generations, which the game squeezes into one life. Early sheep had no woolly fleece for weaving; that came thousands of years later.
Aurochs bulls stood nearly two metres tall and were ferocious. DNA studies suggest Near Eastern cattle may descend from only about 80 aurochs cows. The game squeezes many generations into one life.
Pigs were domesticated at least twice, in Anatolia and in China. They eat almost anything, including human scraps, which suits village life. The game squeezes many generations into one life.

There are hundreds of large animal species, but only a few dozen ever became truly domestic. The ones that did tend to eat many plants, grow fast, breed in pens, stay calm, and live in herds with a leader.

In early farming villages like Çatalhöyük nearly every house looks alike, and archaeologists see little inequality. But once animals, grain stores and land could pile up and be inherited, gaps between families began to form.
Many human diseases began in animals. Living close to herds, and crowded into villages, made it easier for germs to jump to people.
The Natufians of the Levant built permanent hamlets and harvested wild grasses before farming. At Ain Mallaha a woman was buried with a puppy about 12,000 years ago.
Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Anatolia has huge carved stone pillars about 11,600 years old, raised by people who still hunted and gathered.
Some of the clearest early domestic goats come from Ganj Dareh in the Zagros, about 10,000 years ago.
Millet was grown in north China from about 10,000 years ago; domestic pigs and crane-bone flutes at Jiahu are about 9,000 years old.
The Yangtze is where rice farming began. Shangshan shows rice use about 10,000 years ago, but fully domestic rice took thousands of years more.

From about 11,000 to 5,000 years ago the Sahara was far wetter, with lakes, hippos and crocodiles. People fished with bone harpoons and made their own pottery from about 10,000 years ago, and later began herding cattle.

Spirit Cave in Pang Mapha, excavated in the 1960s, holds traces of Hoabinhian people about 12,000–7,500 years ago. Its plant remains were once read as early farming; most scholars now see them as gathered wild plants.
Kuk Swamp in Papua New Guinea shows drainage ditches for gardens from about 10,000–7,000 years ago, one of the places farming began independently, with bananas grown by about 7,000 years ago.
Smoke rises from the round houses at dawn.
Gazelles race along the foothills; the children run after them.
The whole hamlet sits grinding wild grass seed on the querns.
A cold wind sweeps down from the plateau.
Everyone walks across the close-packed roofs.
The sheep graze along the stream.
Wild goats climb the sheer cliffs with ease.
Snow still lies on the peaks though it is spring.
The wind lifts yellow loess dust over the valley.
The millet heads bow with grain.
Herons wade the marsh at dawn.
The marsh rises after a night of heavy rain.
Hippos call in the lake at night.
After weeks of rain the grass grows over your head.
Someone paints giraffes on the rocks by the lake.
Gibbons call across the valley at dawn.
Thick mist hangs low over the stream.
Everyone carries bamboo tubes of water up to the cave.
A bird of paradise dances on a high branch.
Rain falls on the mountains almost every afternoon.

Within a few thousand years, villages like yours will grow into towns. To the south, in Mesopotamia, farmers’ descendants will build the first cities and write the first script; some scholars think writing began with clay tokens for counting sheep and goats. Another line of your descendants will carry wheat and goats into Europe.
The millet and rice of your rivers will one day feed billions. Farmers from here will move south, carrying rice and pigs into Southeast Asia, including today’s Thailand, about 4,000 years ago.

About 5,000 years ago the rains fail and the Green Sahara turns to desert. People drive their cattle to the Nile and to the south; some think Saharan herders were among the roots of Egyptian civilisation.
Farmers from the north will arrive thousands of years later with rice, pigs and dogs. Descendants of foragers like you will mix with them, and the DNA of Southeast Asians today carries both lines.

New Guinea highlanders have gardened their valleys for nearly ten thousand years, to this day, yet the island had no large animal that could be herded; pigs arrived thousands of years later. Geography limited the choices, not the people.
For years the rain grows scarce and the winters long. The elders say they have never seen the like.

About 8,200 years ago a vast flood of meltwater from a North American ice lake entered the ocean, cooling and drying the world for nearly two centuries; some Near Eastern villages were abandoned or changed their ways.
Your family’s plots double in size
Mice creep into the grain store every night
You open the grain store and eat what you saved
Your family’s herd has grown so large the village has started to talk
You train two cattle to drag a wooden sledge of sheaves home from the fields
Evidence for cattle hauling loads this early is thin and debated; ploughing with oxen is clear only thousands of years later.
The aurochs calf grows fast. One day it tosses you to the ground.
The wild young you raised join the domestic herd, bringing new blood into it.
DNA shows early domestic animals kept interbreeding with wild ones for a long time.
You wonder which wild animal would live with people, if you raised its young from birth.
You go back to other work for now.

never hunting the females in birthing season
sharing grain and meat at the harvest feast
a common store kept by the elders
telling the children every year of the land that sank

Some anthropologists suggest human language evolved partly so we could talk about other people: in groups too big to know everyone directly, who can be trusted is learned by word of mouth. It is a hypothesis, not a settled conclusion.
No one knows for sure how religious belief began, and it surely did not begin the same way everywhere. This scene simulates how one person’s explanation might become something a whole group lives by.
Demand the things back, and more
You get back more than you lost.
A public apology is much harder than gossip, but everyone remembers that you made it.
Be glad you accused no one
You overhear people saying your family has many animals but never shares.
People are saying your visions are just a way to make a name for yourself.
People are saying you have started acting as if you stand above everyone.
Hold a feast and share meat with every house
Share your food and things with others
The gossip falls quiet, at least for now.
Go and talk to whoever started it
You speak so plainly that they admit they went too far.
The confrontation only makes things worse.
A story no one answers becomes true in the ears of those who hear it.
You walk away. Some call it calm; others, cowardice.
An elder who wants to teach
An elder has watched you for years. One day she calls you to sit beside her and asks what you want to learn.
Keep it between the two of you
After the disaster everyone sits by the fire asking why. Some of them turn to you.
Say the sky is warning us; we must dance to appease it before every storm season
The next year, before the storms, everyone comes to dance without being told.
Some believe, some laugh. The next year only a few come to dance.
Say it simply happened; no one is to blame
The answer comforts no one, but no one is blamed.
The herds that were once easy to hunt grow smaller every year. People ask you what to do.
Many hunting peoples have taboos, such as not hunting in certain seasons or places, which can help animals recover; how such rules arose in the Stone Age is unknown.
Forbid hunting females in birthing season
Everyone grumbles but obeys. Years later the herds are thick again, and no one remembers who began the rule.
Some obey; some still hunt in secret.
The hunting pays again, but everyone walks farther every year.
Do nothing; they will come back
The next year there are still few.

Early farmers’ skeletons at many sites are shorter and have more tooth decay than foragers’, yet their numbers grew fast, because settled life meant more children. No one could see where this choice led within one lifetime.
Next season you stand over seedlings you planted yourself, and feel you must stay to guard them.
Sow, but keep moving with the seasons
Sometimes you return for the harvest, sometimes not, but you eat better than before.
No. The old life is good
You go on following the herds and seasons, like every ancestor before you.

In many later herding societies, lending animals binds families together: the borrower owes a debt of gratitude and helps when you are in trouble. Whether the first villagers did this is unknown; this part is a simulation.
Word of your generosity reaches every house.
You want to share your life with someone from another house, but their family wants proof you can provide.
Giving animals to the other family at marriage is found in many later herding societies, for example in East Africa. Whether the first villagers did so is unknown; this part is a simulation.
Married, with a gift of animals
Their family welcomes you, and the three animals become the talk of the village.
Work a year in their household
The hardest year of your life, ending in a wedding.
Ask an elder to speak for you
The elder’s words weigh more than any herd.
The harvest went well and people from other villages are coming. You have enough animals for a feast everyone will remember.
Göbekli Tepe holds enormous quantities of animal bone; many archaeologists think great feasts were how many groups were brought together to work.
Feasts where a host gives away great amounts of food are a way of building prestige and social ties found in many societies worldwide.
The fires blaze all night; strangers sing songs you have never heard. They will remember your name.
A small feast for the family
Keep the animals so the herd grows
Your herd grows, but some guests go home disappointed.
This morning two animals are gone from the pen.
The tracks lead to a thicket where both animals are caught. You lead them home.
The tracks vanish on stony ground.
Two animals are not worth a feud.
Your parents have died, leaving all their animals to you.
Once animals and land could be inherited, wealth began to build up across generations, and dividing an inheritance became a source of family quarrels that lasts to this day.
Take them and care for them well
Your herd grows, but the house is quieter.
Take most, since you cared for them more
Everyone is surprised, and no one forgets.
A wildcat in the grain store
A wildcat comes every night to catch the mice in the grain store. It is not very afraid of people.

Cats probably domesticated themselves, drawn to the mice that ate village grain. At Shillourokambos on Cyprus, about 9,500 years ago, a cat was buried near a person; cats are not native to Cyprus, so people must have carried them across the sea.
Let it stay, and leave it scraps
Within months the mice are gone, and the cat sleeps by the hearth.
It vanishes into the dark, and the mice return.
The neighbours’ dog has five puppies. One follows you home every day.
Dogs were bred from wolves thousands of years before farming. At Ain Mallaha in the Levant, about 12,000 years ago, a woman was buried with her hand resting on a puppy. Dogs guard herds from wolves.
It grows up and barks whenever anything nears the pen.
A nanny goat has milk to spare after weaning, so you try milking her into a bowl.

Milk fats in pots from northwest Anatolia are about 8,500 years old. Almost no adults then could digest milk sugar; souring it or making cheese reduces that sugar. Adult milk digestion spread thousands of years later.
Leave it to sour, then eat it
Made soured milk for the first time
Strangely sour, but it sits well and keeps for days.
You let the nanny feed her young.
Animals in the herd begin to cough and droop; some will not graze.
The rest of the herd is saved.
Too late; it is already through the herd.
Butcher the sick ones before they die
A few days later you come down with a fever.
Hold a rite for the herd
In a few days the animals are grazing again. Everyone says the rite worked.
Several die, but the rite lets everyone feel they did all they could.
This year some houses have grain and animals to spare, and some have almost nothing. The elders call everyone to agree what to do.
Propose sharing at the harvest feast every year
The rule is passed down as the ancestors’ teaching, though it began with your words.
Propose that each house keep its own
Hard-working families gain; unlucky ones struggle more.
No one can agree on anything.
Propose a common store kept by the elders
The common store saves everyone in dry years, and gives whoever holds it more power each year.
Everyone fears the store-keepers will cheat.
The stone pillars on the hill
People from many groups gather on a hilltop to cut huge limestone pillars and carve animals on them.

Göbekli Tepe was raised about 11,600 years ago by people who still hunted and gathered. Some pillars stand over 5 metres, carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures. It led some archaeologists to ask whether shared ritual came before farming rather than after.
A hundred people pull together, and the pillar slowly rises. You feel part of something bigger than your band.
Carve a fox on the pillar
Carved an animal on a Göbekli Tepe pillar
Ten thousand years later someone will stand before this fox and wonder who carved it.
Lead the rite on the hill
Every band falls silent when you begin to sing.
You chase a kid goat until you tumble in the dust; the grown-ups roar with laughter.
The whole village helps re-plaster the house floors before the rains.
At harvest everyone sleeps in the fields to keep birds and boar away.
A stranger from another valley brings seeds you have never seen, to trade.
The first Near Eastern crops, such as wheat, barley, lentils and flax, were brought into cultivation in several places and traded between valleys; not every village had to invent them.
You paddle a dugout onto the lake and spear fish with a bone harpoon.
A group of herders drive their cattle to the lake. You have never seen cattle that follow people.
Whether cattle herding in North Africa came from the Near East or also began locally is still debated. Saharan rock art is full of cattle.
You gather areca nuts, beans and gourds from the forest and carry them up to the cave.
Plant remains from Spirit Cave, such as areca, beans and gourds, were once read as early farming, but most scholars later saw them as gathered from the wild.
You strike river pebbles into one-sided tools, as everyone in your band does.
Pebble tools flaked on one face are the hallmark of the Hoabinhian, found across Southeast Asia, including many caves in northern and western Thailand.
Everyone digs drainage ditches in the swamp, so the soil is dry enough for taro.
An elder plays a flute made from a crane’s wing bone; its sound carries across the village.
Crane-bone flutes from Jiahu, China, about 9,000 years old, can still be played today.
Everyone works to raise the village’s great stone wall and tower.
The stone tower of Jericho, about 10,000 years old and some 8 metres tall, is one of the oldest large structures. Whether it was for floods, enemies or ritual is still debated.

At Jericho and Tell Aswad, about 10,000–9,000 years ago, people buried the dead under house floors, then lifted the skulls and modelled faces on them in plaster, with shells for eyes. At Ain Mallaha a woman was buried with a puppy.
At Çatalhöyük the dead were buried beneath the sleeping platforms inside houses, so the living slept above their ancestors every night. Some were dusted with red ochre.
Graves at Jiahu, China, about 9,000 years ago, sometimes held crane-bone flutes and turtle shells filled with pebbles.
At Gobero in Niger, people buried their dead beside an ancient lake that is desert today, some with ornaments.
At many Hoabinhian sites the dead were buried curled up, sometimes with red ochre or stone tools.
There is no clear evidence of how New Guinea highlanders of this time treated their dead; this is a simulation.
Bury them beneath the house floor, to stay with the family
Every night the family sleeps above them, as if they never left.
A year later, lift the skull and model a face in plaster
The plaster face has shell eyes. It is set in the house for the grandchildren to see.
Lay a bone flute beside them
No one will play that flute again.
Bury them with the dog they loved
Their hand rests on the dog, as it did in life.
Bury them curled up under red ochre
The red looks warm against the cold earth.
You are buried beneath the house floor. A year later your descendants lift your skull, give it a plaster face with shell eyes, and set it in the house.
You are buried beneath the floor where you slept. Your family goes on living above you every day.
The band buries you curled as if asleep, under red ochre.
The shore where the elders camped as children is under water now, and every year the sea creeps closer.

As the ice melted the sea rose over 100 metres; about 14,500 years ago it rose especially fast, some 15–20 metres in a few centuries. Nearly half of Sundaland, which joined the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and Borneo, went under. The coastal camps of its people now lie beneath the sea, and we know almost nothing of them.
The upland forest is strange, but the ground stays under your feet.
Stay and fish the new shallows
Fish crowd the drowned mangroves, but every storm pushes the water deeper.
Tell the children of the land that sank
The children ask when the sea will stop. You cannot say, but your story will outlast the shore.
The elders say a great village of the ancestors lies beneath the sea, with houses of stone and fires that never die. One night, at an unusually low tide, you see a faint light far out over the water.

This is made up. Some have claimed Sundaland held an advanced civilisation that sank, but no archaeology supports it; what really drowned were coasts where foragers and fishers lived. Many Southeast Asian peoples have great-flood myths, which some think may remember the rising sea, though that cannot be proven.
Swam toward the light under the sea ✦
The water is icy, and the light is gone when you come near, but in your hand is a green stone bead you cannot explain.
From that night, the story of the village under the sea has one more witness.
A wide grassland stretches east until the far forest is out of sight; herds of banteng graze in the distance.

During glacial times the climate was drier than today. Some researchers propose a corridor of grassland through the heart of Sundaland, a highway for people and animals rather like the African savanna, though this is debated and it may have been open woodland mixed with grass.
A great herd of elephants crosses the river, the calves holding their mothers’ tails.
The Sunda plains now under the sea were home to elephants, rhinos, tapirs, tigers, banteng, wild water buffalo, and orangutans living much farther south than today.
The band burns patches of forest edge; the next year edible plants come up thick.

At Niah Cave in Borneo, evidence from about 50,000–40,000 years ago shows people managing rainforest with fire and knowing how to remove toxins from certain plants before eating them, a remarkably sophisticated knowledge.
A tiger circles the camp all night. No one dares to sleep.

in the season of ripe fruit

The One with the Smallest Hands
You shape riverside clay into a little cup and sneak it beside the fire until it hardens.

The sky stays strangely hazy for months and the sunsets burn blood-red. That winter is colder than any the elders remember.
Toba on Sumatra erupted about 74,000 years ago, one of the largest eruptions known. Its effect on people is debated; sites in Africa and India show people lived through it.
Lived through the year Toba erupted
One of your children falls gravely ill. You nurse them through the night until the fever breaks.
One of your children falls ill and dies. The band buries the little one near camp under red ochre, then sits with you through the night.
One of your children falls ill and dies. The band sits with you through the night.
That night you should have died. The black stone in your hand splits in two, and you wake at dawn.
Because of your words, someone took the blame for a disaster no one could control.
✦ Legend: thousands of years later, people still tell how the ancestors once sent a messenger to tell the story of the world. Your name is lost, but the story lives on.
Your visions are retold among many bands until they become part of a creation story no one remembers who first told.

One of your children falls ill and dies. The family lays the little body in a clay jar beneath the house floor.

About 5,000 years ago Uruk may have been the largest city in the world, with perhaps 40,000–80,000 people. The earliest inscribed tablets come from the Eanna temple of the goddess Inanna. Legend says the city’s wall, some 9 km long, was built by Gilgamesh.

At Ur in the 1920s the archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Cemetery, about 4,600 years old, including the tomb of Queen Puabi. The city’s great ziggurat was built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE.
Lagash and neighbouring Umma fought over the border fields for generations; the Stele of the Vultures records a Lagash victory. Many stone statues of its ruler Gudea were found here.

Nippur was the religious heart of Sumer, home of the god Enlil, but never a political capital. Huge numbers of school tablets were found here; much of the Sumerian literature we know comes from Nippur.
The Sumerian King List says that after the great flood, kingship first came down from heaven at Kish. The same list names Kubaba, a woman tavern keeper who became king of Kish.

At Sippar lived the naditu women of the god Shamash. They did not marry and lived in a cloister of the temple, yet they bought land, lent silver and made contracts in their own names; thousands of tablets record their business.
Babylon rose under Hammurabi (about 1792–1750 BCE) and was greatest under Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE), who built the Ishtar Gate.

In Mesopotamian cities, surplus food could feed people who did not farm. Temples and palaces employed craftsmen, scribes and labourers and paid them in barley, oil and wool. Children usually followed their parents’ trade. A list of professions from the Uruk period names more than a hundred.
a great household, close to the temple and palace
a free family of the city
temple workers, paid in rations of barley

Mesopotamian society was layered. Hammurabi’s laws distinguish free citizens, commoners and slaves, and the same offence carried different penalties. Many people worked for a temple or palace in return for rations. Some slaves were war captives; others fell into slavery through debt.
Wrote a clay tablet with your own hand
A temple scribe writes your name in the list of those who receive rations. You cannot read it, but that is your name.
Ordinary people were listed in ration lists, contracts and receipts, so we know the names of tens of thousands of Mesopotamians who were not kings.
Your name was written on a clay tablet
You pay off the loan with interest, and the scribe smashes the loan tablet.
You cannot pay the debt. The creditor takes you to work it off in his household.
Hammurabi’s law 117 says that a person sold or bound into service for a debt must be freed in the fourth year.
In Mesopotamia a person who could not repay might have to work for the creditor, or sell a child or themselves into debt slavery.
The term is over. You go home a free person again.
The ruler Uru-inimgina proclaims debts forgiven, and forbids the powerful to seize the donkeys, houses and fish of the poor.

The reform texts of Uru-inimgina of Lagash, about 2350 BCE, use the word amargi, literally “return to the mother”, for releasing people from debt. It is often called the oldest written word for “freedom”.
Word comes that a man named Sargon of Akkad is taking the Sumerian cities one by one and tearing down their walls.
Sargon of Akkad (about 2334–2279 BCE) united Mesopotamia into the first empire we know of. Akkadian began to replace Sumerian in government.
For years in a row the northern rains fail, the rivers fall, and herders from the mountains raid the plains for food.

About 4,200 years ago much of the world turned severely dry. Many scholars link it to the fall of the Akkadian Empire and the arrival of the Gutians from the Zagros, though how much it caused is debated.
The whole city lays millions of bricks into a stepped mountain for the moon god. King Ur-Nammu comes to watch.
The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built about 2100 BCE, a core of mud brick faced with baked brick set in bitumen. Its restored base still stands in Iraq today.
An army from Elam breaks into the city. The temples burn; people are killed and carried off; the king is led away a captive.
Ur was sacked by the Elamites about 2004 BCE. The poem known as the Lament for Ur mourns bodies lying in the city gates. Fires that burned cities sometimes baked clay tablets hard and preserved them.
An official reads King Hammurabi’s laws aloud in the market. Each begins: “If a man…”
Hammurabi’s code, about 1754 BCE, has some 282 laws carved on a black stone stele over two metres tall, now in the Louvre. Older law collections exist too, such as Ur-Nammu’s, about 2100 BCE.
A Hittite army from far away storms Babylon, loots the temples and carries off the statue of Marduk.
About 1595 BCE the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon, ending Hammurabi’s dynasty.
Captives from Judah are settled by the canals outside the city. In the evenings you hear them singing sad songs about home.
Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem in 597 and 586 BCE and deported many Judeans to Babylonia. Psalm 137 begins “By the rivers of Babylon”.
The Persian army of King Cyrus enters Babylon almost without a fight, and the priests of Marduk welcome the new king.
In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great took Babylon; the Cyrus Cylinder claims Marduk chose him. Babylon never again ruled an empire of its own, but people went on writing cuneiform there for centuries.
You help load boats at the quay and earn a shekel of silver.

Mesopotamians measured value in silver, by weight. A shekel weighed about 8 grams; in the Old Babylonian period a month’s hired labour cost about one shekel. In daily life people often paid in barley.
a child of a great household
